import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 89

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/89](https://www.erdosproblems.com/89)
- [Er46] Erdős, Paul. On sets of distances of $n$ points. Amer. Math. Monthly
  53 (1946), 248--250.
- [GuKa15] Guth, Larry and Katz, Nets Hawk. On the Erdős distinct distances
  problem in the plane. Ann. of Math. (2) 181 (2015), 155--190.
- [Mo52] Moser, Leo. On the different distances determined by $n$ points.
  Amer. Math. Monthly 59 (1952), 85--91.

### AI disclosure

Lean 4 code in this file was drafted with assistance from OpenAI Codex.
The mathematical content and references are the author's own work.
-/

open Filter
open EuclideanGeometry

namespace Erdos89

/--
Erdős [Er46] asked whether every set of $n$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^2$
determines $\gg \frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}$ many distinct distances.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_89 :
    (fun (n : ℕ) => n/(n : ℝ).log.sqrt) =O[atTop] (fun n => (minimalDistinctDistances n : ℝ)) := by
  sorry

/--
Guth and Katz [GuKa15] proved that there are always $\gg \frac{n}{\log n}$
many distinct distances.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_89.variants.n_dvd_log_n :
    (fun (n : ℕ) => n/(n : ℝ).log) =O[atTop] (fun n => (minimalDistinctDistances n : ℝ)) := by
  sorry

/--
The square grid construction, going back to Erdős and Moser, shows that
$\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}$ is the correct order if the conjecture is true:
there are configurations whose number of distinct distances is
$O(\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}})$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_89.variants.grid_upper_bound :
    (fun n => (minimalDistinctDistances n : ℝ)) =O[atTop]
      (fun (n : ℕ) => n/(n : ℝ).log.sqrt) := by
  sorry

/--
This theorem provides a sanity check, showing that the main conjecture (`erdos_89`) is strictly
stronger than the solved Guth and Katz result. It proves that, trivially, if the lower bound
$\frac{n}{\sqrt{\log n}}$ holds, then the weaker lower bound $\frac{n}{\log n}$ must also hold.
-/
@[category test, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_89.variants.implies_n_dvd_log_n (h : type_of% erdos_89) :
    type_of% erdos_89.variants.n_dvd_log_n := by
  refine .trans ?_ h
  have := (Asymptotics.isLittleO_one_left_iff ℝ).mpr <| tendsto_norm_atTop_atTop.comp <|
    (tendsto_rpow_atTop (show 0 < 1/2 by norm_num)).comp
    (Real.tendsto_log_atTop.comp tendsto_natCast_atTop_atTop)
  convert! (Asymptotics.isBigO_refl (fun n : ℕ ↦ n/(n : ℝ).log) _).mul this.isBigO using 1
  · simp
  · simp_rw [Function.comp, div_mul, ← Real.sqrt_eq_rpow, Real.div_sqrt]

-- TODO(firsching): formalize any remaining remarks from the erdosproblems.com page.

end Erdos89

reformulations.difference: States the conjectural lower bound using Big-O of n/√(log n) against minimalDistinctDistances, rather than quantifying explicitly over every n-point planar set.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The minimum ranges over a nonempty set of natural-number distance counts for every n, and is attained. Its apparent real-valued set-builder expression elaborates to equality between natural counts cast to ℝ; injectivity of the cast preserves the intended minimum. A lower bound on this minimum is equivalent to the same bound for every n-point configuration. Nonnegativity removes the norms in Big-O, and reciprocating its positive constant gives the source's lower-bound convention. The minimum is positive for n≥2, so finite exceptions can be absorbed into the constant. Review89.conjecture_global_iff in /workspace/review/minimum.lean proves equivalence to ∃ c>0, ∀ n≥2, ∀ S : Finset ℝ², S.card=n → c*(n/√(log n)) ≤ distinctDistances S.

reformulations.difference: Expresses the Guth–Katz uniform lower bound through the minimum distance-count function and an asymptotic Big-O relation.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The attained-minimum characterization converts the bound into a universal statement about configurations. For n≥2, log n is positive; the real norms and reciprocal-constant convention therefore give exactly a positive constant times n/log n as a lower bound. Finite exceptions can be absorbed because the minimum distance count is positive for n≥2. Review89.guth_katz_global_iff proves the equivalence to the explicit uniform point-set statement, without using either sorry'd lower-bound theorem.

reformulations.difference: Encodes the existence of configurations with O(n/√(log n)) distances as an upper bound on minimalDistinctDistances, without explicitly constructing the grid.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Because the minimum is attained, an upper bound on it is equivalent to existence of an n-point configuration satisfying that bound; conversely the minimum is no larger than any configuration's count. Review89.grid_upper_global_iff proves equivalence to ∃ C>0, ∀ n≥2, ∃ S : Finset ℝ², S.card=n ∧ distinctDistances S ≤ C*(n/√(log n)). The source's grid construction also covers nonsquare n by selecting n points from a sufficiently large square grid; Erdős's original proof explicitly constructs at least n lattice points. Thus the quantification over arbitrary n does not introduce a stronger claim.

review.notes: Checked all four declarations and the imported distance, minimum, Euclidean-space, logarithm, square-root, filter, and Big-O definitions. Scratch proofs verify empty/singleton counts, minimum attainment, positivity for n≥2, two-point distance counts, and the three statement equivalences. Computable squared-distance grid checks also passed. The existing implication theorem has no sorryAx dependency; /workspace/review/rates.lean independently proves n/log n = o(n/√(log n)). The source still marks the main problem open and confirms both research-solved bounds. Moser's full text was unavailable, but no declaration's mathematical verification depends solely on it: the grid upper bound is explicit in Erdős (1946), Theorem 1.
